summary: Post-2000 wave 1. Philip C. C. Huang becomes a person entry (involution, with Geertz and Chayanov as his acknowledged resources; founding editor of Modern China, 1975), and his exchange with Pomeranz (2002–2003) is drawn once as two critique arrows. Kenneth Pomeranz gains his named critics (Brenner and Isett, Allen and colleagues, Broadberry, Guan and Li) and his 2014 AHA address; Lynn Hunt her political-culture, practical-realism, human-rights and global-era work, with Geertz’s influence moved onto her entry and Moyn’s and Bell’s critique; Lorraine Daston her moral economies of science and her 2009 critique of science studies, with Foucault and Thompson connections; Catherine Hall her imperial and slavery histories, Williams’s influence, her critique of Hobsbawm and Said’s review. Each of the five ends with at least five edges and at least ten dated points, with post-2000 work and reception separated.
authorization: User, 2026-10-17: “Pomeranz is thin too; we need to go back to everyone who kept working after 2000”; “anyone important enough to be featured in the main timeline should have more than one edge and more than one or two points on the timeline”; and “Philip Huang” (added to wave 1). Research: data/extension-2026/post2000-wave1-2026-10-17/evidence-pomeranz.md, evidence-huang.md, evidence-hunt.md, evidence-daston.md, evidence-hall.md.
rationale: The five entries stopped at 2000 (or 1987–1992) under the original 1920–2000 frame, with one to three edges each and no point after 2000; Huang appeared only as a roster name described through Pomeranz. Every edge rests on the person’s own words or a named reader’s explicit statement, read in full or in part with pages; WebFetch extractions and reviewer-only readings are labelled. Weak or held items are left out (kuhn → Huang, Daston → kuhn, Hall → nationaltradition). Robert Brenner is not yet an entry; his critique with Isett stays inside the economic → Pomeranz arrow. Edge_354 is retargeted from political to lynn_hunt because its claim is her acknowledged use of Geertz. Reviewed by Sol (release/sol-review-1.144.md, accept with fixes); the fixes are listed in release/fixes-1.144.md. Findings of an independent second research pass (evidence-*.pass2.md) that rest on texts it read were added and are listed in release/pass2-additions-1.144.md.

edge_899.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own argument, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). He takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as 'Why wasn’t the Yangzi Delta England?' and argues 'that Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path', a result avoided through 'sharp discontinuities, based on both fossil fuels and access to New World resources' (p. 13). 'Constraints connected to energy, and ultimately to quantities of land (particularly the shrinking forests of core areas throughout Eurasia), were a far more important looming impediment to further growth' than capital (p. 19). The Atlantic trade mattered for 'how much they relieved the strain on Europe’s supply of what was truly scarce: land and energy', and 'the fruits of overseas exploitation were probably roughly as important to at least Britain’s economic transformation as its epochal turn to fossil fuels' (p. 23). The book uses 'the fruits of overseas coercion' to explain the difference from China and Japan, 'not the whole of that development' (p. 4). Cooper's 2000 review (read in full) summarises it in the same year: 'Europe had more institutional slack, easier access to coal (which was crucial, in the author's view), and cheap imports of sugar and cotton harvested by slaves in its New World colonies', and objects that Pomeranz 'relies heavily on plausible guesstimates'. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993) already argued, in the publisher's description, 'that the development of certain regions entailed the systematic underdevelopment of other regions'; Bianco (1996, p. 243, read) notes that it 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', including Huang's involution model. A contribution, not a founding: earlier arguments from colonial extraction (Williams 1944, Frank 1969, Amin 1974) are cited at p. 3, n. 2, and he notes parallels with Sugihara (p. 12). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge. Revision 1.144: the critiques now have their own arrows (philip_huang → kenneth_pomeranz; economic → kenneth_pomeranz). Pomeranz restated the timing in 2003: "a gathering consensus, pace Huang, about the timing of that divergence" (JAS 62:1, p. 179, read). Catherine Hall reads the coal-and-colonies argument as part of "a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians": "Pomeranz sees the Atlantic slave-economy and the availability of coal as the two complementary factors allowing Britain to expand" (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014, p. 24, read).

edge_898.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own statement of method, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). Comparisons between scattered core regions should be 'truly reciprocal' (p. 8), 'viewing both sides of the comparison as “deviations” when seen through the expectations of the other, rather than leaving one as always the norm' (p. 8). With Tilly's 'encompassing comparison', 'comparison and the analysis of connections become indistinguishable' (p. 10). 'Thus the book combines comparative analysis, some purely local contingency, and an integrative or global approach', and before 1800 'we have, instead, a polycentric world with no dominant center' (p. 4). The introduction ends 'with connections and interactions explaining what comparison alone cannot' (p. 25). He places the book as 'joining the burgeoning field of “world history,”' while warning that it 'treats the world’s regions very unevenly' and that 'adding a few Chinese and Japanese foils to a European story does not make it “world history”' (p. 25). A contribution, not a founding: the approach was 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong' (p. 7), and 'Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed' (p. 8); the encompassing comparison is Tilly's (p. 10, n. 14). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge. Revision 1.144: later reception of the method. Pomeranz was a co-founding editor of the Journal of Global History, which began publication in 2006 (AHA biography, as the second research pass reads it). Its editors wrote in 2021 that the Great Divergence debate "was a major inspiration for the foundation of the Journal in 2006" and that "comparisons and connections" had been "elaborated perhaps most fruitfully in the context of large-scale reciprocal comparisons" (Frankema, Sood and Tworek, JGH 16:1, pp. 1–2, read in full by the second pass); they do not name Pomeranz.

text_revisions.old: A historian of China whose reciprocal comparisons of Eurasian core regions recast the divergence of European and Chinese economies. The Great Divergence (2000) takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as the reverse question and argues that 'Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path'. Coal, and land-intensive goods from New World colonies worked by enslaved people, relieved Europe's constraints of land and energy. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993) traces the economic and ecological costs for inland North China when the late Qing and Republican state abandoned many hinterland areas.
text_revisions.new: A historian of China whose reciprocal comparisons of Eurasian core regions recast the divergence of European and Chinese economies. The Great Divergence (2000) takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as the reverse question and argues that 'Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path'. Coal, and land-intensive goods from New World colonies worked by enslaved people, relieved Europe's constraints of land and energy. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993), in its publisher’s description and Bianco’s review, traces the economic and ecological costs for inland North China when the late Qing and Republican state abandoned many hinterland areas. The Great Divergence became central to the debate over the “California School”. Philip Huang answered that England and the Yangzi delta stood “at opposite poles” of development and involution (2002–2003); Brenner and Isett located England’s divergence in early modern social-property relations (2002); Broadberry and Gupta found the advanced parts of Asia closer to Europe’s stagnating periphery in wages and prices (2006); Allen and colleagues disputed urban real-wage parity between the Yangzi delta and England (2011); and Broadberry, Guan and Li placed the divergence between leading regions around 1700 (2021). He was a co-founding editor of the Journal of Global History (2006), and his AHA presidential address (2014) asked how history might be reframed “for a less national age”.

The Making of a Hinterland is checked at contents level and through Bianco's 1996 review, read in full; its text is unread. text_revisions.old: Reassesses the explanatory models of social history in her introduction to The New Cultural History. She recognizes turns toward culture within Marxist and Annales histories while questioning the priority assigned to social experience.
text_revisions.new: A historian of the French Revolution whose Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984) joined revolutionary symbols and rhetoric to the sociology of political actors, using Geertz’s interpretive frame, and whose introduction to The New Cultural History (1989) reassessed the explanatory models of social history, recognising turns toward culture within Marxist and Annales histories while questioning the priority assigned to social experience. With Joyce Appleby and Margaret Jacob she defended a “practical realism” (1994), and with Victoria Bonnell she edited Beyond the Cultural Turn (1999). In her AHA presidential address (2003) she asked how the Revolution could “produce such contradictory consequences” as terror, democracy and human rights. Inventing Human Rights (2007), which reviewers summarise as tracing rights to imagined empathy, novels and the rejection of torture, was contested by Samuel Moyn and David A. Bell. Writing History in the Global Era (2014), the book around which this atlas was first developed, argued, in her reviewer’s summary, that globalization had become a new paradigm that could wash away the gains of cultural history.

text_revisions.old: Connects the cultural turn to disputes within social explanation. Hunt authored this introduction and edited the collection; she did not author all its essays. Her political-culture work remains a separate inherited context.
text_revisions.new: Connects the cultural turn to disputes within social explanation. Hunt authored the 1989 introduction and edited the collection; she did not author all its essays. Her political-culture work rests on the existing reading of the 1984 book’s chapter openings, and her later revolution argument on the 2003 address read through the AHA web text. Inventing Human Rights and Writing History in the Global Era are presented through their reviewers (Moyn, Bell, McClure); the books themselves are unread here. The atlas’s Identity histories grouping is her later classification and does not make her its founder. No human-rights entry exists; the 2007 book is drawn as a contribution to cultural history and as the object of a critique.

text_revisions.old: With Peter Galison, investigates changing scientific ideals of objectivity through images and atlas-making. Their 1992 article distinguishes mechanical objectivity from other historically formed components of the concept.
text_revisions.new: A historian of science who historicizes the categories of scientific knowing. Her books include Classical Probability in the Enlightenment (1988) and, with Katharine Park, Wonders and the Order of Nature, 1150–1750 (1998). In “The Moral Economy of Science” (1995) she argued that certain forms of empiricism, quantification and objectivity “require moral economies”, “a web of affect-saturated values”, drawing on Elias’s civilizing process and distinguishing her sense of the term from E. P. Thompson’s. With Peter Galison she studied objectivity itself: their 1992 article distinguishes mechanical objectivity from other historically formed components of the concept, and their book Objectivity (2007) treats it, in reviewers’ readings, as one epistemic virtue beside others rather than their successor. She was a director at the Max Planck Institute for the History of Science from 1995 until 2019. In 2009 she argued that the history of science had become “a discipline” while science studies remained “undisciplined”, and that “to historicize the category of the fact, objectivity, or proof is not thereby to debunk it”.

text_revisions.new: Classical Probability in the Enlightenment (1988); with Peter Galison, “The Image of Objectivity” (1992); “The Moral Economy of Science” (1995); with Katharine Park, Wonders and the Order of Nature, 1150–1750 (1998); with Peter Galison, Objectivity (2007); “Science Studies and the History of Science” (2009); Rules: A Short History of What We Live By (2022). text_revisions.old: Adds a substantive history-of-science contribution beyond gender history. Galison retains equal authorship and argument credit. Their historical analysis does not assert that scientific objectivity is simply impossible.
text_revisions.new: Adds a substantive history-of-science contribution beyond gender history. Galison retains equal authorship and argument credit for the 1992 article and the 2007 book, and Park for Wonders. Their historical analysis does not assert that scientific objectivity is simply impossible: in 2009 she wrote that “‘If historical, then relative’ is a non sequitur”. The 1995 and 2009 essays are read in her own words; Objectivity and Rules remain unread: their content is mediated by reviewers (Switzer and Henning; Lahav) and Rules by its publisher’s description, and the 1988 and 1998 books are dated from her 2009 author note and the Collège de France biography and carry no argument here. “Historical epistemology” in her sense is not the French tradition of the atlas’s Historical epistemology entry, and no edge connects them.

text_revisions.old: With Leonore Davidoff, relates English middle-class formation to gender, family, religion and economic life in Family Fortunes. Class identities and gender relations are investigated together rather than in separate historical accounts.
text_revisions.new: A historian of gender, class, race and empire. With Leonore Davidoff she related English middle-class formation to gender, family, religion and economic life in Family Fortunes (1987), investigating class identities and gender relations together rather than in separate accounts. Civilising Subjects (2002), whose “central argument”, she wrote, “is that being a colonizer was part of the construction of Englishness”, followed Birmingham abolitionists and Baptist missionaries to Jamaica; she credited C. L. R. James with showing what can be gained by studying “metropole and colony in one lens”. Angela Woollacott (2006) reads it as postcolonial history for its “insistence on the interconstitutive connections between colony and metropole”, and Edward Said (2003) praised it while asking for subaltern voices. From 2009 she led, with her research associates Nicholas Draper and Keith McClelland, University College London’s Legacies of British Slave-ownership project, tracing the slave-owners compensated at emancipation into Victorian Britain. In 2014 she and her coauthors identified a move toward modified versions of Williams’s thesis among economic historians, and she argued, against the British Marxist historians’ neglect of “race, slavery and the Caribbean”, that gender and race shaped the formation of capital. Lucky Valley (2024) turns to Edward Long and “racial capitalism”.

text_revisions.old: Family Fortunes: Men and Women of the English Middle Class 1780–1850 (1987). Joint work; retain all coauthor credits.
text_revisions.new: With Leonore Davidoff, Family Fortunes: Men and Women of the English Middle Class 1780–1850 (1987); White, Male and Middle Class (1992); with Keith McClelland and Jane Rendall, Defining the Victorian Nation (2000); Civilising Subjects: Metropole and Colony in the English Imagination, 1830–1867 (2002); Macaulay and Son: Architects of Imperial Britain (2012); with Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland, Katie Donington and Rachel Lang, Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014); “Gendering Property, Racing Capital” (History Workshop Journal, 2014); Lucky Valley: Edward Long and the History of Racial Capitalism (2024). Joint works; retain all coauthor credits. Readings: Said (2003); Gikandi, Levine and Holt (JBS, 2003, as Hall answers them); Woollacott (2006); Tao Wei (2014).

text_revisions.old: Equal coauthor credit with Davidoff. The 1987 work is distinct from Hall’s later introduction and later imperial history. Newly checked evidence is the indexed prologue abstract and publisher description of a later edition.
text_revisions.new: Equal coauthor credit with Davidoff for Family Fortunes, whose newly checked evidence is the indexed prologue abstract and publisher description of a later edition. Family Fortunes and her imperial and slavery work (2002–2014) are distinct projects linked by attention to gender, class and race. The Legacies of British Slave-ownership is collective work and its edges credit the team. Her 2014 History Workshop Journal essay is read in her own words; Civilising Subjects is presented through her own 2003 reply to its commentators (pp. 530–537, read by a second research pass), Said’s and Woollacott’s readings and its publisher description; the commentators’ own texts are unread; Legacies is read through its jointly written introduction in excerpts without print pages and UCL’s 2014 impact case study; Macaulay and Son through Tao Wei’s review; White, Male and Middle Class, Defining the Victorian Nation and Lucky Valley through contents or publisher descriptions only. She is not Stuart Hall.

strand.title: Moral economies of science
strand.focus: Certain forms of empiricism, quantification and objectivity rest on collectively held, affect-laden values, “a web of affect-saturated values”; Daston distinguishes this sense of “moral economy” from Thompson’s and draws on Elias for the self-discipline of observers.
